overview:
Kenya sits on the equator on the east coast of Africa, with the Indian Ocean on one side and Lake Victoria on the other. It is about the size of Texas and borders Ethiopia, Somalia, Tanzania, Uganda, and South Sudan. The capital, Nairobi, is a high-altitude city of glass towers, bustling markets, and a national park inside the city limits where giraffes graze with skyscrapers in the background. Mombasa on the coast is a historic port of Swahili culture and coral-stone old town.

About 55 million people live in Kenya, from more than 40 ethnic groups. English and Swahili are the official languages, and most Kenyans speak a third language at home. Kenya is a presidential republic and East Africa's economic hub, known for tea and coffee exports, flowers flown to Europe, and a mobile-phone money system that spread across the world. Tourists come for the great wildebeest migration and safaris among lions and elephants, and Kenyan runners dominate the world's marathons.
landAndNature: The Great Rift Valley slices through Kenya from north to south, a trench edged by cliffs and dotted with lakes; Lake Nakuru and Lake Bogoria glow pink with hundreds of thousands of flamingos. Mount Kenya, an extinct volcano with glaciers on the equator, is Africa's second-highest peak at 5,199 meters. The Maasai Mara grasslands in the southwest host the annual migration of more than a million wildebeest and zebras crossing from Tanzania, chased by lions and crocodiles. Amboseli's elephants walk beneath Kilimanjaro, just over the border. The north is hot desert around Lake Turkana, the world's largest desert lake. The coast has coral reefs, mangroves, and white beaches. Kenya's Big Five are lions, leopards, elephants, buffalo, and rhinos, and it is one of the best places on Earth to see them.
peopleAndCulture: Kenya's peoples include the Kikuyu, Luhya, Kalenjin, Luo, Kamba, Maasai, and Swahili, each with its own language and traditions; the Maasai are known for red shukas, beaded jewelry, and high jumping dances. Most Kenyans are Christian, with a Muslim community on the coast. Ugali, a stiff corn porridge, is eaten with sukuma wiki greens, beans, or nyama choma, roasted meat shared with friends, and chai tea is drunk all day. Kenya is the world's greatest running nation: Kalenjin athletes from the high Rift Valley have won countless Olympic and marathon titles, and Eliud Kipchoge ran the first marathon under two hours in 2019. Rugby sevens and soccer are also popular, and Nairobi's music mixes benga guitar with hip-hop.
history: Some of the oldest human fossils and stone tools have been found around Lake Turkana, earning Kenya the name cradle of humankind. Bantu and Nilotic peoples settled the interior over the past 2,000 years, while Arab and Persian traders built Swahili towns on the coast, such as Lamu, from the 700s. Portugal seized the coast in the 1500s, and Britain took control of the interior in the 1890s, building a railway to Uganda and settling white farmers in the highlands. The Mau Mau uprising of the 1950s was harshly suppressed but hastened independence, which came on December 12, 1963 under Jomo Kenyatta. Daniel arap Moi ruled for 24 years, and multiparty democracy returned in 1992. A new constitution in 2010 spread power to counties.
funFacts: Nairobi is the only capital city in the world with a national park inside it, where lions and rhinos live 7 kilometers from downtown.
Kenyan runner Eliud Kipchoge became the first person to run a marathon in under two hours, in Vienna in 2019.
Kenya's mobile money system, launched in 2007, lets people pay for almost anything by phone and was copied worldwide.
Turkana Boy, a nearly complete 1.6-million-year-old skeleton, was found near Lake Turkana in 1984.
During the great migration, over a million wildebeest cross the Mara River, where crocodiles lie in wait.
